strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to inform training decisions. Decomposing loss by token position offers an interpretable connection between context availability and training dynamics.

The empirical investigation is substantial. It includes models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, ID and OOD evaluation, and additional GPT-NeoX and MoE experiments. Importantly, Figures 3 and 5 evaluate future-loss prediction from training prefixes, rather than relying exclusively on retrospective curve fitting, and show consistent improvements over the included baselines.

The data-mixture experiment provides practical evidence beyond fitting accuracy: the selected mixtures improve final perplexity at both evaluated model sizes and outperform the comparison on 12 of 14 downstream results.
The equations, architecture tables, package versions, and prediction pseudocode provide a useful foundation for understanding and implementing the approach.
weaknesses: The decisive methodological concern is that the comparisons do not isolate the benefit of token-position modeling. The proposed predictor incorporates the known learning-rate schedule and a piecewise transition, whereas the aggregate-loss baselines lack these features. Once a0 and a1 are fixed, Equation 10 reduces to a constant plus a2(N), making a schedule-aware aggregate-loss baseline particularly important. Without this control, the central attribution of improved prediction to finer granularity remains unresolved.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is promising but insufficient to establish reliable ranking. Selection uses 10B tokens, only 2.5% of training, while the forecasting experiments begin at 10%. The paper does not report predicted versus observed final losses across all five candidates or ranking uncertainty. Table 5 improvements are approximately 0.7–1.3% in perplexity, without uncertainty estimates; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish variability across independent runs.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in consequential places. The outlier-removal threshold, nonlinear-fitting initialization and constraints, evaluation frequency, and actual candidate mixture weights are unspecified, and no implementation or loss-trace release is identified. Algorithm 1 also applies the Equation 15 calibration when Npred <= Nsep, whereas Section 2.4 requires observations after Nsep. These ambiguities affect the forecasting procedure itself.

A direct numerical inconsistency undermines confidence in the baseline comparison: Section 2.3 reports power-law R² below 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, while Table 9 reports R² above 0.95 for 67% of checkpoints on the 58M model. The manuscript needs to reconcile these results and explain any differences in fitting protocols.

The theoretical interpretation exceeds what is established. Equation 17 follows from manually freezing a0 and a1; it does not independently prove equal learning across positions or justify uniform weighting. Figure 11 and the suppression experiments support narrower empirical observations. Appendix C also rejects exponential decay after setting its additive asymptote to zero, although an exponential with a positive offset satisfies the stated nonzero-loss requirement.

Novelty and generality need more precise framing. Kaplan et al. already investigate training-step dependence, and the schedule-aware loss-prediction work cited in Appendix H deserves substantive comparison. Most evidence concerns one corpus, tokenizer, and cosine training recipe; the linear-schedule experiment demonstrates retrospective fit after changing the functional form, not forecast generalization. The supported contribution is therefore narrower than a generic temporal law for decoder LLMs. Together with the comparison and reproducibility concerns, this leaves the case close but insufficient for a clear Findings recommendation.
